hints: Picture the three types of orbital shapes you know and recall which one has two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus.
walkthrough:
Visualise what a p orbital looks like**
Think of an s orbital as a simple sphere around the nucleus. A p orbital is different. It has two equal lobes, one on each side of the nucleus, meeting at the nucleus where there is a node. You can draw it as a figure of eight or dumbbell.
Final answer: Dumbbell shape / vertical figure of eight centred on the nucleus.

hints: Recall that first ionisation energy always starts from one mole of isolated gaseous atoms and removes one electron to form a 1+ ion.
walkthrough:
Build the ionisation equation from the definition**
First ionisation energy is the energy to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. So start with $\mathrm{Si(g)}$, show loss of one electron as $\mathrm{e^{-}}$, and form $\mathrm{Si^{+}(g)}$. Both silicon species must be gas state because the atoms are isolated and not bonded.
Final answer: $\mathrm{Si(g) \rightarrow Si^{+}(g) + e^{-}}$

hints: Think about what changes in the atom as you move from Na to Ar in Period 3, protons, shells and shielding.
Link the change in protons with similar shielding to the pull felt by the outer electron.
walkthrough:
Track protons and shells across the period**
Moving across Period 3 each element adds one proton to the nucleus and one electron to the same outer shell (n = 3). The inner shells (1 and 2) stay the same, so the extra shielding from inner electrons is almost constant.

Connect stronger pull to higher ionisation energy**
With more protons pulling and almost the same shielding blocking that pull, the effective attraction on the outer electron increases. The electron is held more tightly, so you must supply more energy to remove it, giving the general increase in first ionisation energy.

Final answer: Across Period 3 nuclear charge / proton number increases while shielding remains similar.
Greater nuclear attraction holds the outer electron more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it.

hints: Look along the graph for the biggest vertical jump in ionisation energy and note between which two electrons removed it occurs.
Recall what a large jump tells you about moving from outer shell electrons to an inner shell closer to the nucleus.
walkthrough:
Spot where the big jump happens**
Read the plot from left to right. The first three points rise only gently, then there is a large jump up to the 4th point. After that the rise is gentle again. That large jump after the third electron is the key evidence.

Translate the jump into outer electrons**
The first three electrons come off relatively easily because they are all in the same outer shell, at similar distance and shielding. The fourth electron needs much more energy because you have broken into a full inner shell which is much closer to the nucleus and less shielded. Three outer electrons means Group 13.

Final answer: group number: 13 (Group 3)
Large increase between 3rd and 4th ionisation energies shows 3 electrons in the outer shell, the 4th electron is removed from an inner shell closer to the nucleus and with less shielding.

hints: Write the weighted mean expression for $A_r$ using 92.2% of mass 28.0 and letting the abundance of $^{29}\mathrm{Si}$ be $x$%, so $^{30}\mathrm{Si}$ is $(7.8-x)$%.
Set your expression equal to 28.09 and rearrange to solve for $x$, the abundance of $^{29}\mathrm{Si}$.
Subtract your value for $^{29}\mathrm{Si}$ from 7.8% to find the abundance of $^{30}\mathrm{Si}$ to one decimal place.
walkthrough:
Set up the $A_r$ equation with one unknown**
Let abundance of $^{29}\mathrm{Si}$ = $x$%. Then abundance of $^{30}\mathrm{Si}$ = $(7.8 - x)$% because together they make 7.8%. The weighted mean is: $$A_r = \frac{(92.2 \times 28.0) + (x \times 29.0) + ((7.8-x) \times 30.0)}{100} = 28.09$$

Find the $^{30}\mathrm{Si}$ abundance**
Simply subtract from the combined total: $$\text{abundance of }^{30}\mathrm{Si} = 7.8 - 6.6 = 1.2\%$$ Give this to one decimal place as requested: 1.2%.

Final answer: $$\frac{(92.2 \times 28.0) + (x \times 29.0) + ((7.8-x) \times 30.0)}{100} = 28.09$$
$x$ = abundance of $^{29}\mathrm{Si}$ = 6.6%
percentage abundance of $^{30}\mathrm{Si}$ = $7.8 - 6.6$ = 1.2%

hints: Use the very high melting point of 1900 degrees C to decide whether only weak intermolecular forces or strong lattice bonds must be broken.
Think about what type of particles must be free to move for a molten substance to conduct electricity.
Combine insolubility, high melting point and non-conduction to choose between ionic, metallic, simple molecular and giant covalent.
walkthrough:
Use melting point to identify lattice strength**
A melting point of $1900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is huge. You are not just overcoming weak van der Waals forces between separate molecules. You must be breaking a network of strong bonds throughout the solid. That points to a giant lattice.

Rule out ionic and metallic using conductivity**
If $\mathrm{Si_3N_4}$ were ionic, the molten liquid would contain free moving ions and would conduct. If it were metallic, delocalised electrons would conduct. It does not conduct when molten, so there are no mobile charged carriers. That fits covalent bonding where all electrons are locked in shared pairs.

Pull the evidence together**
High melting point plus insolubility plus electrical non-conduction in the melt is classic for a giant covalent structure. Strong covalent bonds extend in three dimensions and need a lot of thermal energy to break, but provide no free ions or electrons for conduction.

Final answer: Giant covalent / giant molecular lattice.
Strong covalent bonds between atoms require large amount of energy to break, giving very high melting point.
No mobile ions or delocalised electrons, so cannot conduct electricity even when molten.

hints: Remember complete combustion in oxygen gives $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$, and any sulfur in the fuel forms $\mathrm{SO_2}$.
walkthrough:
Balance C, H and S then O**
$\mathrm{C_2H_5SH}$ contains 2 C, 6 H and 1 S. So you need $2\mathrm{CO_2}$ for carbon, $3\mathrm{H_2O}$ for hydrogen and $1\mathrm{SO_2}$ for sulfur. Count O atoms on the right: $4 + 3 + 2 = 9$, so you need $4\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}$ on the left. The balanced equation is $\mathrm{C_2H_5SH + 4\frac{1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 3H_2O + SO_2}$.

hints: Recall what gas $\mathrm{SO_2}$ forms when it dissolves in rain water and what general pollution problem this causes.
Think of one specific damage caused by increased acidity, to lakes, forests, soil or buildings.
walkthrough:
Link $\mathrm{SO_2}$ to acid rain**
$\mathrm{SO_2}$ is an acidic gas. When it mixes with water vapour and oxygen in the atmosphere it forms sulfurous acid and is further oxidised to sulfuric acid, which falls as acid rain.

Describe one concrete harm**
Extra acidity has real effects. For example, it lowers the pH of rivers and lakes which kills fish and other aquatic life, or it damages leaves and leaches nutrients and toxic $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ from soil harming trees, or it weathers limestone buildings and statues. Any one well described consequence earns credit.

Final answer: Forms acid rain as $\mathrm{SO_2}$ dissolves / reacts with rainwater to form sulfurous / sulfuric acid.
Consequence e.g. lowers pH of lakes / rivers killing fish / damages trees / crops / leaches aluminium ions from soil / erodes buildings / statues.

hints: Count the total moles of gas on the left side of $\mathrm{SO_2(g) + O_3(g) \rightleftharpoons SO_3(g) + O_2(g)}$ and compare with the right side.
Recall how Le Chatelier predicts the shift when pressure increases if both sides have the same number of gas moles.
walkthrough:
Count gas moles on each side**
On the left you have $1 + 1 = 2$ moles of gas ($\mathrm{SO_2}$ plus $\mathrm{O_3}$). On the right you also have $1 + 1 = 2$ moles of gas ($\mathrm{SO_3}$ plus $\mathrm{O_2}$).

Apply Le Chatelier for pressure**
Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles to reduce pressure. Here both sides have the same number, so there is no shift in either direction. The composition of the equilibrium mixture stays the same.

Final answer: No effect on composition / position of equilibrium.
Equal moles of gas on both sides (2 mol to 2 mol), so increased pressure favours neither forward nor reverse reaction.

hints: Check the sign of $\Delta H$ for $\mathrm{3SO_2(g) + O_3(g) \rightleftharpoons 3SO_3(g)}$ to decide if the forward reaction takes in or gives out heat.
Recall which direction Le Chatelier shifts the equilibrium when you raise temperature for that type of reaction.
walkthrough:
Read the enthalpy sign**
$\Delta H = +462.3 \, \mathrm{kJ mol^{-1}}$ is positive, so the forward direction ($\mathrm{SO_2}$ to $\mathrm{SO_3}$) is endothermic. It takes in heat.

Choose temperature to favour product**
Raising temperature adds heat. By Le Chatelier the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to absorb the extra heat. That means shifting right, making more $\mathrm{SO_3}$. So any temperature above the given 300 K will increase the yield.

Final answer: Forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H$ = +462.3 $\mathrm{kJ mol^{-1}}$).
Increase temperature / any temperature higher than 300 K shifts equilibrium to the right to absorb heat, increasing yield of $\mathrm{SO_3}$.
